title: Tennessee's Long Game
author: Aneesh Sohoni
summary: Aneesh Sohoni opens with new research showing Tennessee rose from 42nd in the nation on NAEP in 2003 to 16th in 2024, the largest climb of any state. He hands the issue to Kevin Huffman, Tennessee's education commissioner from 2011 to 2015, who lists what he thinks drove the results. Huffman credits the Bredesen administration for acknowledging poor results and raising standards, then describes his own team's work on Race to the Top implementation. His list includes a public, ambitious goal of becoming the fastest-improving state, accountability aligned from teachers to department staff, a relentless focus on talent, quality curricula and training, and expanded options for families in low-performing schools. He frames education policy as a relay race across governors of both parties. Sohoni's takeaway is that lasting change is collective change that requires evidence, willingness to change course and persistence.
points: Tennessee climbed from 42nd to 16th on NAEP between 2003 and 2024, the largest gain of any state, through sustained rather than one-off effort.
Naming the problem honestly and raising standards, even at the cost of lower scores, was a critical first step.
A public, ambitious goal set before results arrived created shared direction and accountability.
Aligned accountability and a relentless focus on talent extended from teachers and principals to state department employees.
Continuity across governors, likened to a relay race, let reforms outlast any single leader.
quotes: That experience taught me something I’ve carried with me ever since: lasting change is collective change.
In 2003, Tennessee ranked 42nd in the country. By 2024, it ranked 16th. That 26-place climb was the largest of any state.

Bredesen and his team led Tennessee’s successful Race to the Top application, bluntly acknowledging that results were poor and needed to change. This acknowledgement of the problem was a critical step that should not be overlooked.
The state set an ambitious goal. We set the goal that Tennessee would be the fastest-improving state in the country on NAEP.
We used law, regulations, a waiver from the federal government — every tool at our disposal. And we used soft accountability again and again, calling out low performance and elevating high flyers.
TDOE focused relentlessly on people and talent. When I was in seat, we were fixated on recruiting, hiring, and managing staff to higher performance.
Governor Haslam always said that education policy is a relay race. He got the baton from Governor Bredesen with a running start.
